lessons.title: What this course is, and what the RTA is
lessons.html:
If you rent the place where you live in Alberta, a provincial law called the Residential Tenancies Act (RTA) sets minimum standards for landlords and tenants. The official Alberta.ca page on rights and responsibilities says the RTA is a framework for how the two sides must treat each other.

When a landlord and tenant agree to rent a home, they enter a residential tenancy agreement. Alberta.ca says this agreement can be written, oral, or implied, but it should be written so both sides have a record. A later page on starting a tenancy says an agreement cannot take away rights set out in the RTA. Anything in an agreement that tries to waive those rights is void.

This course is a map of official pages. It does not tell you what to do in your dispute. It does not write your notice or fill in an RTDRS form. The Centre for Public Legal Education Alberta (CPLEA) also publishes Renting 101 and related pages. CPLEA says that guide provides general legal information on Alberta law only. Use it as extra reading, not as a replacement for Alberta.ca or for advice about your own case.

If you rent only the land under a mobile home, a different law (the Mobile Home Sites Tenancies Act) may apply. Read the official page for that situation.

For questions, Alberta’s Consumer Contact Centre is listed on the official contact page (see Lesson 5).

lessons.title: Responsibilities of tenants and landlords
lessons.html:
Even if a duty is not written in your rental agreement, Alberta.ca says landlords and tenants must still meet the RTA.

Tenants must:

  • pay rent on time
  • be considerate of the landlord and other tenants
  • not endanger other tenants
  • not perform illegal acts or conduct illegal business on the rental premises
  • keep the rental premises reasonably clean
  • prevent damage to the rental premises
  • move out when the rental agreement ends
  • follow the rules in the agreement that do not conflict with the RTA

Landlords must:

  • make the rental premises available on the date the agreement takes effect
  • give the tenant a written “notice of landlord” within 7 days of the tenant moving in, or post that notice in a visible place in a common area
  • not disturb the tenant’s peaceful enjoyment of the premises (for example, not bother the tenant beyond what is needed to do the landlord’s business)
  • keep the premises habitable at the start and throughout the tenancy (the page gives examples such as no bed bugs and working heat)

“Habitable,” on that page, means the premises meet the Minimum Housing and Health Standards under the Public Health Act and Housing Regulation.

Required notices must be delivered in person or by registered mail, unless the official page’s other service rules apply. Tenants should use the mailing address on the notice of landlord.

This list is general information from the live page, not a judgment about your building. If the premises do not feel safe or healthy, the official contact page also points tenants to Alberta Environmental Public Health. This course does not file that complaint for you.

lessons.title: Agreements, deposits, and inspection reports
lessons.html:
Alberta has two main kinds of rental agreements. A fixed-term tenancy begins and ends on specific dates. A periodic tenancy has a start date but no end date (often month-to-month). Either side may end a periodic tenancy by giving notice, following the official rules.

Landlords usually ask for a security deposit (sometimes called a damage deposit). As of November 2026, Alberta.ca said the deposit cannot be more than one month’s rent at the time the tenancy starts. It cannot be increased later if the rent goes up. Landlords must put the deposit into an interest-bearing trust account in Alberta within 2 banking days of collecting it. Tenants can ask for a receipt. Check the live page; these details can change.

When the tenancy ends, tenants have the right to get the deposit back, with any interest owing, if there is no damage beyond normal wear and tear, the place has been properly cleaned if the agreement requires it, and no rent or other costs are owing. Normal wear and tear means deterioration that happens over time with use, even with reasonable care.

Move-in and move-out inspection reports are mandatory. They describe the condition of the home when you move in and when you move out. You can use them to show you did not cause damage that was already there. If the inspection-report rules are not met, the landlord cannot deduct damages or cleaning costs from the deposit (the landlord may still try to recover costs another way). Keep copies.

This course does not calculate your deposit or complete your inspection form.

lessons.title: Ending a tenancy and getting a deposit back
lessons.html:
How a tenancy ends depends on the type of agreement. A fixed-term tenancy ends on the date in the agreement. Alberta.ca says neither side needs to give notice to end it on that date (though telling each other early is described as a good practice, not a legal requirement). Unless you both agree otherwise, the tenant must move out by noon on that end date.

To end a periodic tenancy, written notice is required. The notice must include the address, the date the tenancy will end, and the signature of the person giving notice. Landlords must also include their reasons. The amount of notice depends on who is giving it and whether the tenancy is weekly, monthly, or yearly. As of November 2026, the page said a tenant ending a month-to-month tenancy must give one full tenancy month of notice, and a landlord must give three full tenancy months. Weekly and yearly tenancies have different times. Always check the live “Ending a tenancy” page. Those times can change, and other rules apply to evictions and “substantial breach.”

Alberta.ca also says tenants cannot withhold rent to force a landlord to do something such as making repairs. The landlord is entitled to have the rent paid in full when it is due.

If there are no deductions, the landlord must return the full deposit plus interest within 10 days after the tenant gave up possession. If there are deductions, the page describes other 10-day and 30-day steps. Date-stamp: November 2026. Provide a forwarding address in writing and keep copies of your papers for 3 years.

This lesson does not draft your notice or tell you whether an eviction notice you received is valid.

lessons.title: Getting help and the RTDRS
lessons.html:
If you have a problem, Alberta.ca says to try to resolve it before filing a complaint or applying for a formal remedy. Talk calmly, write down what was said, and keep copies of letters or emails. State facts. Do not include threats.

If you believe a landlord has committed an RTA offence, you can contact the Service Alberta / Consumer Contact Centre to ask about an investigation. As of November 2026, the contact page listed: 780-427-4088, toll-free 1-877-427-4088, and rta@gov.ab.ca, weekdays 8:15 am to 4:30 pm (closed statutory holidays).

If the issue is still not resolved, a tenant or a landlord may apply to the Residential Tenancy Dispute Resolution Service (RTDRS), or they may go to court. RTDRS can deal with concerns such as ending a tenancy, unpaid rent or utilities, security deposits, damages, repairs, and other common disagreements. As of November 2026, the overview said you can apply within 2 years from the date the claim or loss first came to your attention, if the claim is under $100,000. Hearings are by telephone. You must file an application, serve the other party, take part in the hearing, and enforce any order. This course cannot predict the result and does not file the application for you.

RTDRS contact listed on that page: 780-644-3000 and rtdrs@gov.ab.ca. The page says RTDRS does not accept applications or evidence at that email address.

CPLEA’s renting pages are extra general information. For a live dispute, get help from official contacts or a legal clinic.
